mcqs.question: A team runs ingestion at 2am and a dependent transform job at 4am using cron, assuming ingestion always finishes in under two hours. What's the specific risk this creates?
options: The transform job will refuse to start until ingestion explicitly signals completion
Cron cannot execute two different jobs on the same server
Cron jobs automatically fail if run within four hours of each other
The transform job may run against stale or incomplete data on any day ingestion runs longer than expected, with no built-in detection
mcqs.explanation: Cron has no concept of dependency between jobs — it only knows fixed times — so if ingestion runs long even once, the transform proceeds anyway on whatever partial data exists, silently, with nothing to flag it. Cron can run any number of jobs on one server without restriction, doesn't impose spacing rules between jobs, and critically has no mechanism to wait for another job's actual completion signal.

mcqs.question: A pipeline depends on a vendor's file drop that arrives at an unpredictable time, sometimes hours later than usual. Which scheduling model best fits this situation?
options: Fixed interval, scheduled for the vendor's typical drop time
Data-driven / sensor-triggered, so the DAG starts only once the file has actually arrived
Event-triggered by a nightly cron job regardless of file status
No scheduling model can handle unpredictable arrival times
mcqs.explanation: A sensor-based trigger waits for the actual signal that the file has landed, sidestepping the unreliability of guessing a fixed time that may not match the vendor's actual delivery pattern. A fixed schedule guessing the typical time would regularly run against missing or incomplete data, and orchestrators handle exactly this unpredictable-timing case well via sensors rather than being unable to address it.

mcqs.question: Why does backfilling a DAG rely on tasks referencing a 'logical date' rather than the actual wall-clock time they run?
options: Wall-clock time is technically impossible for an orchestrator to access
Logical dates are only used for documentation purposes and have no effect on task behavior
So a task triggered later for a past date behaves identically to how it would have behaved on that date, rather than reading 'today' relative to the real current time
Logical dates eliminate the need for any retry configuration during a backfill
mcqs.explanation: Tying a task's logic to its logical date rather than real time is exactly what lets a backfill triggered today for March 3rd produce the same result as if it had actually run on March 3rd — without that, a backfilled task run today would incorrectly read 'yesterday' relative to today instead of relative to March 3rd. Logical dates have real behavioral effect on task logic, orchestrators can access wall-clock time freely, and retry configuration is a separate, still-relevant concern during backfills.

mcqs.question: What's the key conceptual difference between Airflow's core abstraction and Dagster's core abstraction?
options: Airflow cannot execute Python code, while Dagster only supports Python
Airflow is fundamentally task-and-order-centric, while Dagster is fundamentally centered on data assets and their dependencies
Dagster does not support scheduling DAGs on a fixed interval
Airflow requires a paid license while Dagster does not have any commercial offering
mcqs.explanation: The distinguishing conceptual difference is what each scheduler reasons about natively — Airflow orders opaque tasks, while Dagster tracks the data assets each step produces and their lineage, which changes how you structure and test pipelines in each. Airflow runs Python tasks extensively, Dagster fully supports fixed-interval scheduling, and licensing model isn't the meaningful distinction being tested here.

mcqs.question: Two separate DAGs each use a sensor to wait on the other DAG's output, creating a deadlock at runtime. Why might neither DAG's own cycle-detection catch this?
options: Cycle detection within a single DAG only examines that DAG's own dependency graph, not cross-DAG waiting relationships established through sensors
Orchestrators never implement any cycle detection at all
Sensors are immune to deadlocks by design
This scenario is impossible to construct in any real orchestrator
mcqs.explanation: Most orchestrators detect true cycles at parse time only within a single DAG's own declared dependencies — a deadlock formed across two separate DAGs each waiting on the other via sensors falls outside that single-DAG validation and can go undetected until it actually deadlocks at runtime. Orchestrators do implement cycle detection, sensors are not immune to this failure mode, and this exact cross-DAG scenario is a real, documented risk rather than an impossible one.

mcqs.question: What operational problem do deferrable tasks solve compared to a sensor that polls in a loop while holding a worker slot?
options: They eliminate the need for the external condition to ever actually occur
They make the DAG's waiting behavior visible to end users for the first time
They free up the worker slot while waiting, preventing many simultaneously-waiting sensors from exhausting orchestrator capacity
They guarantee the external condition will be met faster than a normal sensor would detect it
mcqs.explanation: The core fix is capacity management — releasing the worker slot during the wait means many DAGs waiting on slow external signals don't collectively starve the orchestrator of workers needed for unrelated, ready-to-run tasks. The DAG still needs the actual condition to occur, the user-visible waiting behavior is the same as a polling sensor, and detection speed of the underlying condition isn't inherently faster, only the resource cost of waiting is reduced.
